findings.title: Map-roles checks ignore manage and admin roles
findings.body: canMapRoles, canMapCompositeRoles, and canMapClientScopeRoles only call hasPermission for that one scope. They do not treat AdminRoles.MANAGE_CLIENTS or a granted MANAGE permission as sufficient, unlike canManage/canConfigure/canView. With ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 enabled, a realm admin or anyone granted manage-clients (or an all-clients manage permission) is denied mapping client roles, composites, and client-scope roles unless a separate map-roles* permission is also granted. That is an authorization regression versus the V1 evaluator and versus the transitive manage behavior already expected for users.

findings.title: Per-client resource hides all-clients permissions
findings.body: hasPermission(ClientModel, scope) loads the resource named by the client id and, if that resource exists, evaluates only that resource. The all-clients resource is consulted only when no per-client resource exists. A client that already has a narrower permission (for example view or configure) will therefore never receive an all-clients manage, view, or map-roles grant, and a negative permission on the type resource will not apply either. Admins who are allowed to manage every client can be forbidden from managing the one client that also has an object-level permission, and the fallback comment in this method is wrong for that case. If getResourceTypeResource returns null, the following findByResource(server, resource) can also NPE instead of denying.

findings.title: Existing admin-permissions clients are not migrated
findings.body: init returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is already set, and nothing else in this change creates the new Clients resource type or the configure, map-roles-client-scope, and map-roles-composite scopes. Realms that already enabled fine-grained admin permissions (Users only) keep the old schema. Creating or evaluating a Clients permission then fails in getOrCreateResource ("No scopes found" / missing type resource) or getScope (scope not in the resource server). Upgraded deployments cannot use the new client permissions without a manual re-init.

findings.title: Client id filter includes the type resource name
findings.body: getClientsWithPermission adds resource.getName() for every Clients-typed resource that grants the scope, including the schema resource whose name is "Clients" rather than a client UUID. Callers that filter the client list by this set will either look up a non-existent client id or, when only an all-clients permission exists, return no clients at all. All-clients access is not expanded to real client ids, so partial-list and query paths that depend on this method are wrong.

findings.title: Client resource names are not resolved
findings.body: getResourceName only special-cases the Users type. Client resources created by resolveClient are stored under the internal client id and typically have no display name, so the method falls through to resource.getDisplayName() and returns null. Admin permission APIs and the UI will show a blank name for a client permission instead of the clientId, and a deleted client is not reported as missing the way a missing user is.

findings.title: V2 does not clean up permissions when a client is removed
findings.body: The removal listener now runs only when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) is enabled. Under V2, management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2 and clients().setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException, so the V1 branch cannot be reused, and no V2 branch deletes the authorization resource named by the removed client id. After a client is deleted, orphaned Clients resources and policies remain on the admin-permissions client and can be matched again if that id is reused or shown as dangling permissions.

findings.title: requireView javadoc describes a boolean return
findings.body: The new javadoc on requireView says it returns true if canView() returns true, and requireViewClientScopes is documented the same way. Both methods are void and are specified elsewhere to throw ForbiddenException. Callers reading only these comments will treat a failed check as a boolean result instead of an authorization failure.
